title: Dow Climbs 150 Points While Nasdaq Slips Amid Ongoing AI Stock Rotation – Live Updates
body:
Wall Street closed Friday with a mixed performance as the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose more than 240 points, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped, underscoring a broader market rotation away from high‑growth technology and artificial‑intelligence (AI) stocks that had fueled a rally earlier in the week. The S&P 500 managed a modest gain, leaving investors to finish a generally down‑beat trading day after a brief burst of optimism on Thursday.

The Dow’s advance was led by heavyweight industrials and consumer‑goods names that posted solid earnings and dividend yields, offsetting the weakness in the tech‑heavy Nasdaq. Companies such as UnitedHealth Group, Home Depot and Chevron each posted gains of between 0.8 % and 1.4 %, buoyed by a combination of better‑than‑expected quarterly results and upbeat forward‑looking guidance. By contrast, the Nasdaq’s decline was driven primarily by a pull‑back in AI‑centric equities, with megacap firms like Nvidia, Microsoft and Alphabet all slipping between 0.5 % and 1.2 % after earlier spikes that had pushed the index to record highs.

Analysts point to a “rotation” that began late Thursday, when investors started trimming positions in speculative AI plays and reallocating capital toward more defensive sectors. “We saw a classic profit‑taking move,” said Laura Chen, senior market strategist at Meridian Capital. “The AI hype cycle generated a lot of upside in a short period, and now traders are looking for a more balanced risk profile as earnings season unfolds.” The shift coincided with a modest uptick in Treasury yields, which nudged the 10‑year note above 4.5 %, adding pressure on growth stocks that are sensitive to higher borrowing costs.

The broader market context adds nuance to the day’s movements. The U.S. economy continues to show resilience, with consumer spending and labor market data remaining robust, yet inflationary pressures have not fully abated. The Federal Reserve’s latest policy stance—maintaining rates at the current 5.25‑5.50 % range while signaling a data‑dependent approach—has left investors navigating a narrow corridor between growth and value. In this environment, sectors such as utilities, health care and industrials have attracted attention for their relative stability and dividend yields, while high‑beta tech names have faced heightened volatility.

From a technical perspective, the Dow’s trajectory suggests it may be testing the upper band of its short‑term trading range, potentially setting the stage for a continuation of its upward drift if momentum holds. The Nasdaq, however, is hovering near a key resistance level around 15,300 points; a breach could reignite the AI rally, while a failure to clear the barrier may invite further downside. Meanwhile, the S&P 500’s modest gain reflects its role as a barometer for the overall market, balancing the divergent forces at play.

Looking ahead, market participants will be closely watching upcoming earnings releases from major AI and cloud‑computing firms, as well as macroeconomic indicators slated for release later this week, including the core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index. A stronger‑than‑expected PCE reading could reinforce concerns about inflation, prompting a further shift toward defensive stocks. Conversely, any signs of slowing demand for AI hardware or services could accelerate the rotation already underway, pressuring the Nasdaq and related growth indices.

In sum, Friday’s mixed results highlight a market in transition, as investors recalibrate after a period of exuberant AI‑driven gains. While the Dow’s rise offers a glimpse of resilience in traditional sectors, the Nasdaq’s pullback signals caution among traders wary of overvaluation and rising rates. The next few weeks will likely determine whether the rotation is a temporary correction or the beginning of a more sustained shift in capital allocation, shaping the narrative for U.S. equities heading into the final quarter of the year.
